items.stem: Which Period 3 element has the highest melting point?
items.answer: silicon
items.markingKey: Si: giant covalent lattice, 1683 K.

items.stem: Explain why the melting point increases from sodium to aluminium.
items.answer: Metallic bonding becomes stronger: charge on the ions increases (+1 to +3), ions get smaller and more delocalised electrons per atom, so attraction is stronger.
items.markingKey: increased ionic charge/smaller ions [1]; more delocalised electrons, stronger metallic bonding [1]

items.stem: Explain why there is a large decrease in melting point from silicon to phosphorus.
items.answer: Si is giant covalent (many strong covalent bonds broken); P is simple molecular P₄ (only weak intermolecular forces overcome).
items.markingKey: Si giant covalent [1]; P weak intermolecular forces [1]

items.stem: Place these Period 3 elements in order of increasing melting point and explain the position of the highest: sodium, phosphorus, magnesium.
items.answer: phosphorus < sodium < magnesium. Magnesium is highest: giant metallic.
items.markingKey: correct order [1]; structure of highest identified [1]; reason (bond type broken on melting) [1]

items.stem: Place these Period 3 elements in order of increasing melting point and explain the position of the highest: sodium, silicon, argon, magnesium.
items.answer: argon < sodium < magnesium < silicon. Silicon is highest: giant covalent (giant molecular).
items.markingKey: correct order [1]; structure of highest identified [1]; reason (bond type broken on melting) [1]

items.stem: Jonas plots a graph of the melting points of the Period 3 elements in an AS practical class. (a) Explain the increase in melting point from Na to Al. (b) Explain why the atomic radius decreases across the period.
items.answer: (a) Stronger metallic bonding: higher charge, smaller ions, more delocalised electrons. (b) Increasing nuclear charge with similar shielding.
items.markingKey: (a) Stronger metallic bonding: higher charge, smaller ions, more delocalised electrons. [2] (b) Increasing nuclear charge with similar shielding. [2]

items.stem: Which Period 3 element is the best electrical conductor?
items.answer: aluminium
items.markingKey: Three delocalised electrons per atom.

items.stem: Explain why the ionic radius increases sharply from Si⁴⁺ to P³⁻.
items.answer: Cations have lost the outer (third) shell; anions have gained electrons and keep three shells, so P³⁻ has an extra shell.
items.markingKey: cations lose outer shell [1]; anions have an extra shell [1]

items.stem: Explain why silicon is a semiconductor.
items.answer: Silicon has a giant covalent structure with no delocalised electrons at low temperature, but a few electrons can be freed on heating, so conductivity is low and increases with temperature.
items.markingKey: giant covalent, electrons localised [1]; small conductivity increasing with T [1]

items.stem: "The melting point of silicon is high because of strong intermolecular forces." Comment on this statement made by a student, correcting any error.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. Silicon is giant covalent: many strong covalent bonds must be broken.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Place these Period 3 elements in order of increasing melting point and explain the position of the highest: silicon, argon, sulfur.
items.answer: argon < sulfur < silicon. Silicon is highest: giant covalent (giant molecular).
items.markingKey: correct order [1]; structure of highest identified [1]; reason (bond type broken on melting) [1]

items.stem: Place these Period 3 elements in order of increasing melting point and explain the position of the highest: sodium, magnesium, chlorine.
items.answer: chlorine < sodium < magnesium. Magnesium is highest: giant metallic.
items.markingKey: correct order [1]; structure of highest identified [1]; reason (bond type broken on melting) [1]

items.stem: The melting points (K) of the Period 3 elements are Na 371, Mg 923, Al 933, Si 1683, P 317, S 392, Cl 172, Ar 84. (a) Explain the low and varied melting points of P, S and Cl. (b) Explain why the atomic radius decreases across the period.
items.answer: (a) Simple molecules P₄, S₈, Cl₂: weak London forces; more electrons in S₈ so highest. (b) Increasing nuclear charge with similar shielding.
items.markingKey: (a) Simple molecules P₄, S₈, Cl₂: weak London forces; more electrons in S₈ so highest. [3] (b) Increasing nuclear charge with similar shielding. [2]

items.stem: The melting points (K) of the Period 3 elements are Na 371, Mg 923, Al 933, Si 1683, P 317, S 392, Cl 172, Ar 84. (a) Explain why the atomic radius decreases across the period. (b) Explain why argon has the lowest melting point.
items.answer: (a) Increasing nuclear charge with similar shielding. (b) Monatomic with only very weak London forces (18 electrons).
items.markingKey: (a) Increasing nuclear charge with similar shielding. [2] (b) Monatomic with only very weak London forces (18 electrons). [1]

items.stem: The melting points (K) of the Period 3 elements are Na 371, Mg 923, Al 933, Si 1683, P 317, S 392, Cl 172, Ar 84. (a) Describe and explain the trend in electrical conductivity across the period. (b) Explain why argon has the lowest melting point.
items.answer: (a) Increases Na → Al (more delocalised electrons); Si semiconductor; P to Ar non-conductors (no mobile charge carriers). (b) Monatomic with only very weak London forces (18 electrons).
items.markingKey: (a) Increases Na → Al (more delocalised electrons); Si semiconductor; P to Ar non-conductors (no mobile charge carriers). [3] (b) Monatomic with only very weak London forces (18 electrons). [1]

items.stem: What is seen when sodium reacts with cold water?
options: a white solid forms on the surface only
it floats, fizzes, melts into a ball and moves around
it sinks and reacts very slowly
items.answer: it floats, fizzes, melts into a ball and moves around
items.markingKey: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂; solution alkaline (pH 13–14).

items.stem: Explain why aluminium appears unreactive with water and oxygen despite its position in the reactivity series.
items.answer: It is covered in a thin, tough layer of aluminium oxide that protects the metal beneath.
items.markingKey: oxide layer [1]; prevents further reaction [1]

items.stem: Explain why magnesium reacts much faster with steam than with cold water.
items.answer: Steam is at a higher temperature, so more molecules have energy ≥ Ea; magnesium oxide forms rather than a hydroxide layer.
items.markingKey: higher temperature/more energy [1]; more successful collisions [1]

items.answer: (a) +2: equal to the number of outer-shell electrons. (b) ionic; dissolves with very slight hydrolysis, pH about 6.5

items.stem: Which equation shows the reaction of magnesium with steam?
items.answer: Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂
items.markingKey: With steam MgO forms; with cold water Mg(OH)₂ forms very slowly.

items.stem: Explain why the maximum oxidation number of Period 3 elements in their oxides rises from +1 to +6.
items.answer: It equals the number of outer-shell electrons used in bonding: Na 1, Mg 2, Al 3, Si 4, P 5, S 6.
items.markingKey: equals number of outer electrons [1]; examples [1]

items.stem: "Magnesium reacts vigorously with cold water to form magnesium oxide." Comment on this statement made by a student, correcting any error.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. Mg reacts very slowly with cold water forming Mg(OH)₂; it forms MgO with steam.

items.stem: Which Period 3 oxide is amphoteric?
items.answer: Al₂O₃
items.markingKey: Reacts with acids and with alkalis.

items.stem: Explain why aluminium oxide is described as amphoteric, giving equations.
items.answer: It reacts with acids: Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O; and with alkalis: Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH + 3H₂O → 2NaAl(OH)₄.
items.markingKey: with acid equation [1]; with alkali equation [1]

items.stem: Explain the trend in the acid–base nature of the Period 3 oxides.
items.answer: Bonding changes from ionic (Na, Mg: basic, contain O²⁻) through amphoteric Al₂O₃ to covalent (Si, P, S: acidic); the electronegativity difference falls across the period.
items.markingKey: ionic basic → covalent acidic [1]; linked to electronegativity/bonding [1]

items.stem: Freya writes in a revision note: "SiO₂ is a basic oxide because silicon is in the middle of the period." Identify the error in this statement and give the correct version.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. SiO₂ is acidic: it reacts with hot concentrated NaOH to form sodium silicate.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: "AlCl₃ dissolves in water like NaCl to give a neutral solution." Comment on this statement made by a student, correcting any error.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. AlCl₃ is covalent and hydrolyses, releasing HCl, so the solution has pH about 3.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Leila adds MgCl₂ to water. Describe the bonding in MgCl₂, what is observed, the approximate pH and write an equation for the change.
items.answer: ionic; dissolves with very slight hydrolysis; pH about 6.5; MgCl₂(s) → Mg²⁺(aq) + 2Cl⁻(aq)
items.markingKey: ionic [1]; observation/hydrolysis or simple dissolving [1]; pH about 6.5 [1]

items.stem: Describe the bonding in Al₂O₃, state how it behaves when added to water, and give the approximate pH of the resulting mixture. Write an equation where a reaction occurs.
items.answer: ionic with covalent character, giant lattice; insoluble, no reaction; pH 7
items.markingKey: bonding: ionic with covalent character, giant lattice [1]; behaviour: insoluble, no reaction [1]; pH 7 [1]

items.stem: Noah is given samples of the oxides Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃, SiO₂, P₄O₁₀ and SO₃ in a quality-control laboratory. (a) Explain why SiO₂ does not dissolve in water but is classified as acidic. (b) Explain the change from basic to acidic oxides in terms of electronegativity.
items.answer: (a) Giant covalent, insoluble; reacts with hot concentrated NaOH forming Na₂SiO₃. (b) Electronegativity difference with O falls across period: ionic oxides give O²⁻ (basic); covalent oxides react to form acids.
items.markingKey: (a) Giant covalent, insoluble; reacts with hot concentrated NaOH forming Na₂SiO₃. [2] (b) Electronegativity difference with O falls across period: ionic oxides give O²⁻ (basic); covalent oxides react to form acids. [2]

items.stem: Arjun is given samples of the oxides Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃, SiO₂, P₄O₁₀ and SO₃ in an AS practical class. (a) Describe the trend in bonding across the oxides. (b) Write two equations to show the amphoteric nature of Al₂O₃. (c) Explain why SiO₂ does not dissolve in water but is classified as acidic.
items.answer: (a) Ionic (Na₂O, MgO), ionic with covalent character (Al₂O₃), giant covalent (SiO₂), simple covalent (P₄O₁₀, SO₃). (b) Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O; Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH + 3H₂O → 2NaAl(OH)₄ (c) Giant covalent, insoluble; reacts with hot concentrated NaOH forming Na₂SiO₃.
items.markingKey: (a) Ionic (Na₂O, MgO), ionic with covalent character (Al₂O₃), giant covalent (SiO₂), simple covalent (P₄O₁₀, SO₃). [2] (b) Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O; Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH + 3H₂O → 2NaAl(OH)₄ [2] (c) Giant covalent, insoluble; reacts with hot concentrated NaOH forming Na₂SiO₃. [2]

items.stem: In a chemistry competition in Karachi, teams identify elements from their properties. Explain how the formula of the highest oxide of a Period 3 element can be used to deduce its group.
items.answer: The oxidation number in the highest oxide equals the number of outer electrons, giving the group (e.g. X₂O₅: +5, Group 15).
items.markingKey: oxidation number from formula; equals outer electrons/group [2]

items.stem: In a chemistry competition in Cape Town, teams identify elements from their properties. (a) Explain how the formula of the highest oxide of a Period 3 element can be used to deduce its group. (b) Explain how the pH of the solution formed when a chloride is added to water helps identify the element.
items.answer: (a) The oxidation number in the highest oxide equals the number of outer electrons, giving the group (e.g. X₂O₅: +5, Group 15). (b) Ionic chlorides of Na/Mg give pH 7 or 6.5; covalent chlorides (Al, Si, P) hydrolyse to give acidic solutions (pH 1–3).
items.markingKey: (a) oxidation number from formula; equals outer electrons/group [2] (b) ionic neutral; covalent hydrolyse acidic [2]

items.stem: Element X is in Period 3. Its element exists as crown-shaped X₈ molecules; It forms two common oxides, XO₂ and XO₃. Identify X and explain how each piece of information supports your answer.
items.answer: X is sulfur (Group 16)
items.markingKey: identifies sulfur [1]; links clue to property [1] links clue to property [1]

items.stem: Which ion has the largest radius?
items.answer: P³⁻
items.markingKey: Anions are larger; P³⁻ has the lowest nuclear charge of the isoelectronic anions.

items.stem: A student in Mumbai compares the structures of Period 3 elements. Explain why silicon is a semiconductor.
items.answer: Silicon has a giant covalent structure with no delocalised electrons at low temperature, but a few electrons can be freed on heating, so conductivity is low and increases with temperature.
items.markingKey: giant covalent, electrons localised; small conductivity increasing with T [2]

items.stem: Place these Period 3 elements in order of increasing melting point and explain the position of the highest: aluminium, phosphorus, sodium.
items.answer: phosphorus < sodium < aluminium. Aluminium is highest: giant metallic.
items.markingKey: correct order [1]; structure of highest identified [1]; reason (bond type broken on melting) [1]

items.stem: Yusuf plots a graph of the melting points of the Period 3 elements in a research laboratory. (a) Explain why silicon has the highest melting point. (b) Explain why argon has the lowest melting point.
items.answer: (a) Giant covalent structure: many strong covalent bonds broken. (b) Monatomic with only very weak London forces (18 electrons).
items.markingKey: (a) Giant covalent structure: many strong covalent bonds broken. [2] (b) Monatomic with only very weak London forces (18 electrons). [1]

items.stem: The melting points (K) of the Period 3 elements are Na 371, Mg 923, Al 933, Si 1683, P 317, S 392, Cl 172, Ar 84. (a) Explain the low and varied melting points of P, S and Cl. (b) Explain why argon has the lowest melting point.
items.answer: (a) Simple molecules P₄, S₈, Cl₂: weak London forces; more electrons in S₈ so highest. (b) Monatomic with only very weak London forces (18 electrons).
items.markingKey: (a) Simple molecules P₄, S₈, Cl₂: weak London forces; more electrons in S₈ so highest. [3] (b) Monatomic with only very weak London forces (18 electrons). [1]

items.stem: What colour flame is seen when sulfur burns in oxygen?
items.answer: blue
items.markingKey: S + O₂ → SO₂.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why magnesium reacts much faster with steam than with cold water. (b) Explain why aluminium appears unreactive with water and oxygen despite its position in the reactivity series.
items.answer: (a) Steam is at a higher temperature, so more molecules have energy ≥ Ea; magnesium oxide forms rather than a hydroxide layer. (b) It is covered in a thin, tough layer of aluminium oxide that protects the metal beneath.
items.markingKey: (a) higher temperature/more energy [1]; more successful collisions [1] (b) oxide layer [1]; prevents further reaction [1]

items.stem: 1.24 g of silicon reacts completely with oxygen: Si + O₂ → SiO₂. Calculate the mass of SiO₂ formed.

Jonas investigates the reactions of magnesium with oxygen, chlorine and water in a quality-control laboratory. (a) Describe what is seen and write an equation for the reaction with oxygen. (b) Write an equation for the reaction with chlorine.
items.answer: (a) burns with a brilliant white flame, white solid; 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO (b) Mg + Cl₂ → MgCl₂
items.markingKey: (a) burns with a brilliant white flame, white solid; 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO [2] (b) Mg + Cl₂ → MgCl₂ [1]

items.stem: A teacher in Kuala Lumpur demonstrates the reactions of magnesium. (a) Write an equation for the reaction with chlorine. (b) Describe the reaction, if any, with water. (c) Describe the bonding in the chloride formed and predict its behaviour in water.
items.answer: (a) Mg + Cl₂ → MgCl₂ (b) Very slow with cold water (Mg + 2H₂O → Mg(OH)₂ + H₂); rapid with steam: Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂ (c) ionic; dissolves with very slight hydrolysis, pH about 6.5
items.markingKey: (a) Mg + Cl₂ → MgCl₂ [1] (b) Very slow with cold water (Mg + 2H₂O → Mg(OH)₂ + H₂); rapid with steam: Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂ [2] (c) ionic; dissolves with very slight hydrolysis, pH about 6.5 [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which Period 3 oxide is amphoteric? (b) What is the pH of the solution formed when sodium oxide is added to water?
items.answer: (a) Al₂O₃ (b) 13–14
items.markingKey: (a) Reacts with acids and with alkalis. (b) Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH.

items.stem: A student in Auckland relates the bonding in oxides and chlorides to their reactions with water. Explain why MgCl₂ gives a slightly acidic solution but NaCl gives a neutral one.
items.answer: Mg²⁺ is small and doubly charged, so it polarises surrounding water molecules and causes slight hydrolysis releasing H⁺; Na⁺ has a low charge density.
items.markingKey: Mg²⁺ higher charge density; slight hydrolysis releasing H⁺ [2]

items.stem: A student in Accra relates the bonding in oxides and chlorides to their reactions with water. Explain why aluminium oxide is described as amphoteric, giving equations.
items.answer: It reacts with acids: Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O; and with alkalis: Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH + 3H₂O → 2NaAl(OH)₄.
items.markingKey: with acid equation; with alkali equation [2]

items.stem: Mohammed adds SiCl₄ to water. Describe the bonding in SiCl₄, what is observed, the approximate pH and write an equation for the change.
items.answer: covalent (simple molecular); hydrolyses vigorously, white solid and fumes of HCl; pH about 1–2; SiCl₄ + 2H₂O → SiO₂ + 4HCl
items.markingKey: covalent (simple molecular) [1]; observation/hydrolysis or simple dissolving [1]; pH about 1–2 [1]

items.stem: Describe the bonding in MgO, state how it behaves when added to water, and give the approximate pH of the resulting mixture. Write an equation where a reaction occurs.
items.answer: ionic, giant lattice; reacts slightly to form Mg(OH)₂; pH about 9; MgO + H₂O → Mg(OH)₂
items.markingKey: bonding: ionic, giant lattice [1]; behaviour: reacts slightly to form Mg(OH)₂ [1]; pH about 9 [1]; equation MgO + H₂O → Mg(OH)₂ [1]

items.stem: A teacher in Karachi asks students to relate the structures of the Period 3 chlorides NaCl, MgCl₂, AlCl₃, SiCl₄ and PCl₅ to their reactions with water. (a) Write an equation for the hydrolysis of PCl₅ and give the pH of the solution. (b) Explain why AlCl₃ gives an acidic solution.
items.answer: (a) PCl₅ + 4H₂O → H₃PO₄ + 5HCl; pH 1–2 (b) Covalent/small highly charged Al³⁺ polarises water; hydrolysis releases H⁺/HCl, pH 3.
items.markingKey: (a) PCl₅ + 4H₂O → H₃PO₄ + 5HCl; pH 1–2 [2] (b) Covalent/small highly charged Al³⁺ polarises water; hydrolysis releases H⁺/HCl, pH 3. [2]
